fields.title: Adoption and frequency: the average describes a user who doesn't exist
fields.keyTakeaway: An overall product average almost always hides two different products. Look at the share of users who reached the action and the frequency distribution, not a single number.
fields.checkQuestion: Average frequency is 3 times a week. What might this hide?
fields.blocks/0/text: The node's key question remains the same — **what is happening in the product** — but now it's about the shape of the data. The exact same average comes from completely different products.
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you don't answer the question.** You optimize for a non-existent average user and fail to notice that you have two segments with opposite behavior.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Two simple slices that almost always change the picture
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **Adoption** — what share of accounts reached the key action at least once.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **Frequency** — how often those who reached it do it; look at the histogram, not the average.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **Separate the denominator.** 'Out of all registered' and 'out of those who reached it' are different questions.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **Look at registration cohorts**, otherwise new accounts dilute the picture for old ones.
fields.blocks/3/text:
Average: 3.1 swaps per account per month.
Broken down: 64% of accounts didn't make a single swap. Among the remaining 36%, the median is 8 swaps per month.

So you don't have a 'product where people occasionally swap shifts', but two products: one is shift scheduling, the other is active shift swapping within the team. The number 3.1 describes neither of them.
fields.blocks/4/text: A month for a weekly scenario is four opportunities. A window that's too short turns normal users into 'inactive'.
fields.blocks/5/text: The distribution shows what is happening, but not why. It tells you which segment to go study — the explanation will come from interviews and feedback, not from the histogram.
